1.title: Data Models and Schema Evolution
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Data Models and Schema Evolution. This module covers the task statement: design data models and schema evolution. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Design schemas for Amazon Redshift, DynamoDB and Lake Formation. Handle changes to the characteristics of data (schema evolution). Perform schema conversion with A W S S C T (Schema Conversion Tool) and A W S D M S (Database Migration Service) Schema Conversion. Establish data lineage with SageMaker M L (machine learning) Lineage Tracking and SageMaker Catalog. Describe indexing, partitioning, compression and other optimization practices. Describe vectorization and how a Bedrock knowledge base uses it.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Models Its Data
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Models Its Data. The warehouse needs fast reports by customer, route and month. The tracking app must fetch a shipment and its latest events by I D. The lake holds telemetry by day, and analysts want one governed table. Your job: design each schema around how the data will be read.

1.title: Amazon Redshift: dimensional design
1.text: Amazon Redshift: dimensional design. The figure shows this: A star schema: a central fact table of shipment measures joined to small dimension tables for customer, route, truck and date. Star schema: a fact table (measures such as weight, cost, delay; foreign keys) joined to dimension tables (descriptive attributes). Snowflake schema normalizes dimensions further (more joins).

1.title: Amazon Redshift: dimensional design, continued
1.text: Amazon Redshift: dimensional design, continued. Choose keys for joins and filters:; Distribution key (key style) on the column used to join the large fact table to a large dimension: co-locates rows and avoids shuffles; all style for small, slowly changing dimensions; even when there is no clear join key; auto lets Redshift decide; Sort key on the column most used in range filters (usually date) so blocks can be skipped; Column compression encoding (auto by default) reduces storage and I O. Primary and foreign key constraints are informational in Redshift: the optimizer uses them, but Redshift does not enforce them.

1.title: Amazon Redshift: dimensional design, continued
1.text: Amazon Redshift: dimensional design, continued. Denormalize for read speed when updates are rare.

1.title: Amazon DynamoDB: design from the access patterns
1.text: Amazon DynamoDB: design from the access patterns. The figure shows this: DynamoDB data modeling: start from the queries, pick a high-cardinality partition key and a sort key, then add secondary indexes for other access patterns. List every access pattern first (get a shipment, list a truck's events by time); design keys to serve them, not the entities. Partition key: many distinct values, evenly used (shipment I D); sort key orders items within a partition and allows range queries (begins with, between).

1.title: Amazon DynamoDB: design from the access patterns, continued
1.text: Amazon DynamoDB: design from the access patterns, continued. Single-table design: several entity types in one table with generic keys (P K (partition key), S K (sort key)), so one query returns related items. Secondary indexes: G S I (global secondary index) (different partition and sort key; own capacity; eventually consistent; add or remove any time), L S I (local secondary index) (same partition key, different sort key; created with the table; shares capacity; strong consistency option). Limits: an item is at most four hundred kilobytes; no joins, so model relationships by key design or duplicate data. Attribute values can be strings, numbers, binary, sets, lists and maps; the table is schemaless apart from the key.

1.title: AWS Lake Formation: lake tables
1.text: A W S Lake Formation: lake tables. Lake Formation governs databases and tables in the Glue Data Catalog over S three: design table schemas with column names and types, partition keys (such as date), file format (Parquet) and location. Add security design: L F (Lake Formation)-tags (attribute-based) and column, row and cell filters (Module fifteen). Separate zones: raw (landing), curated (clean, typed), consumption (aggregated), with catalog databases per zone. Exam tip: "Large fact table joined to a large dimension on customer id" to key distribution on customer id for both. "Queries filter by date ranges" to sort key on the date column. "DynamoDB table needs a second way to query" to a global secondary index.

1.title: Schema Evolution and Changing Data
1.text: Schema Evolution and Changing Data. Schema evolution equals the structure of data changes over time: new columns, removed columns, renamed or retyped fields, new partitions, new sources. Principles: additive changes are safest (add optional fields with defaults); avoid renaming and changing types in place; version schemas; test before release.

1.title: Schema Evolution and Changing Data, continued
1.text: Schema Evolution and Changing Data, continued. Formats. Avro, Parquet, O R C (Optimized Row Columnar) and Jason carry or tolerate added columns; C S V is positional and breaks easily; Iceberg supports add, drop, rename and reorder columns and partition evolution without rewriting data. Glue Schema Registry. Central, versioned schemas (Avro, Jason Schema, Protobuf) for Kafka, M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka), Kinesis, Flink and Lambda; compatibility modes (backward, forward, full, the all variants, none, disabled) reject unsafe versions; the registry is serverless and free. Glue crawlers. Choose update behavior (update the table or ignore) and delete behavior when schemas drift. Glue jobs. DynamicFrames tolerate mixed types (ResolveChoice); handle new columns explicitly.

1.title: Schema Evolution and Changing Data, continued
1.text: Schema Evolution and Changing Data, continued. Redshift. alter table add or drop column; some type changes (for example widening V A R C H A R) are in place; others need a deep copy. DynamoDB. Schemaless: new attributes need no migration; changing keys needs a new table or index. Athena or Glue tables. Add columns at the end; schema-on-read exposes new fields. Backward compatible: new consumers can read old data; forward compatible: old consumers can read new data; full: both. Other changes to data characteristics: volume, velocity and quality shift: repartition, resize, re-index, add validation (Module thirteen). Exam tip: "Producers add fields to events and consumers must not break" to A W S Glue Schema Registry with backward (or full) compatibility. "Table must add, rename and drop columns on a data lake without rewriting files" to Apache Iceberg.

1.title: Schema Conversion
1.text: Schema Conversion. Schema conversion translates tables, views, indexes, procedures and functions from a source database engine to a different target engine (for example Oracle or S Q L Server to PostgreSQL or Aurora), usually the first step of a heterogeneous migration. A W S D M S Schema Conversion: a managed feature in the D M S console: it assesses how much converts automatically, converts the schema and code, and lets you apply it to the target.

1.title: Schema Conversion, continued
1.text: Schema Conversion, continued. A W S S C T (Schema Conversion Tool): the desktop application that does the same and produces an assessment report; code that cannot be converted is flagged for manual work [A W S S C T was removed from the exam's in-scope service list but the skill still names it]. Order: assess to convert schema to apply to target to migrate data with A W S D M S (full load and C D C (change data capture)). Homogeneous migrations (same engine) need no conversion: use native tools or D M S. Exam tip: "Migrate an Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL" to convert the schema (D M S Schema Conversion or S C T), then move the data with D M S.

1.title: Data Lineage
1.text: Data Lineage. Data lineage records where data came from, what happened to it, and where it went: sources to transformations to outputs. Why: trust and debugging ("why is this number wrong?"), impact analysis (what breaks if this table changes), audits and compliance (prove the origin), reproducibility. A W S tools:; Amazon SageMaker Catalog captures and shows lineage across assets in SageMaker Unified Studio, so people can trace a dataset to its sources and consumers; Amazon SageMaker M L Lineage Tracking records the steps and artifacts of M L workflows (data sets, training jobs, models, endpoints) so a model can be traced to its training data.

1.title: Data Lineage, continued
1.text: Data Lineage, continued. Capture options: job and pipeline logs, catalog metadata, and naming and tagging standards; combine with CloudTrail (who did it) and A W S Config (what changed). Exam tip: "Show which source datasets and jobs produced a report" to lineage in SageMaker Catalog. "Trace a model back to the data and job that trained it" to SageMaker M L Lineage Tracking.

2.title: Indexing, Partitioning, Compression and Optimization
2.text: Indexing, Partitioning, Compression and Optimization. Indexing. What it does: A lookup structure that avoids scanning everything. Where: R D S (Relational Database Service) or Aurora B-tree indexes; DynamoDB G S I or L S I; Redshift sort keys and zone maps; OpenSearch inverted and vector indexes. Partitioning. What it does: Splits data by key so queries read only needed parts. Where: S three prefixes (year equals or month equals ) with Athena, Glue, Redshift Spectrum; DynamoDB partitions by partition key; Kinesis shards, Kafka partitions. Compression. What it does: Smaller files, less I O. Where: Parquet or O R C with Snappy or Zstandard; Redshift column encodings; gzip for text. Columnar formats. What it does: Read only needed columns. Where: Parquet, O R C (Module three).

2.title: Indexing, Partitioning, Compression and Optimization, continued
2.text: Indexing, Partitioning, Compression and Optimization, continued. File sizing. What it does: Fewer, larger files (about one hundred twenty-eight megabytes to one gigabyte). Where: Compaction jobs, Iceberg maintenance. Bucketing or clustering. What it does: Group related rows in files. Where: Athena and Hive bucketing; Redshift sort and distribution. Denormalization and aggregation. What it does: Precompute joins and rollups. Where: Materialized views, aggregate tables. Caching. What it does: Keep hot results close. Where: Dax (DynamoDB Accelerator), MemoryDB, query result caching. Partition design rules: pick keys that queries filter on (usually date), with moderate cardinality; too many tiny partitions hurt, too few huge ones scan too much; keep layouts consistent. Trade-off: every index or copy speeds reads but costs writes and storage. Exam tip: "Athena scans too much data" to partition by the filter column, use Parquet, compress and compact files.

2.title: Vectorization Concepts
2.text: Vectorization Concepts. The figure shows this: Vectorization and retrieval: split documents into chunks, embed them into vectors, store them in a vector index; at question time embed the question, retrieve the nearest chunks, and add them to the prompt. Vectorization converts text, images or other data into vectors (embeddings) with an embedding model; similar meaning to nearby vectors.

2.title: Vectorization Concepts, continued
2.text: Vectorization Concepts, continued. A knowledge base for Amazon Bedrock automates the pipeline for retrieval-augmented generation (R A G):; Ingest documents from a data source (for example S three); Split into chunks (a chunking strategy); Embed each chunk with an embedding model; Store vectors and the link to the source in a vector index (OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, and other supported vector stores); Sync when documents change (re-ingest); At query time: embed the question, retrieve the most similar chunks, add them to the prompt, and let the model answer.

2.title: Vectorization Concepts, continued
2.text: Vectorization Concepts, continued. Choices: chunk size (too small loses context, too large dilutes meaning), embedding dimension (matches the model, for example one thousand twenty-four for several models), float or binary vectors (binary uses one bit per dimension: cheaper, less precise), metadata filters. R A G (Retrieval Augmented Generation) adds private knowledge without retraining the model. The vector store is a data store like any other: it needs access control, encryption, refresh and monitoring. Exam tip: "Give a foundation model access to private documents without retraining it" to R A G with a Bedrock knowledge base and a vector store.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Redshift schema: Star schema; key dist on the join column, all small dims, even or auto. DynamoDB schema: Access patterns first; high-cardinality partition key plus sort key; single-table design. Lake Formation: Catalog tables with types, partitions, Parquet, location; raw or curated or consumption zones; L F-tags. Schema evolution: Additive and optional changes; Avro or Parquet or Iceberg. Schema conversion: D M S Schema Conversion (managed) and S C T (desktop): assess to convert to apply to D M S data; heterogeneous only. Lineage: Source to transform to output; SageMaker Catalog (assets) and M L Lineage Tracking (M L). Optimization: Index, partition, compress, columnar, one hundred twenty-eight megabytes to one gigabyte files, materialized views, cache; every index costs writes. Vectorization: Chunk to embed to vector index to retrieve to augment prompt (R A G); float thirty-two versus binary; Bedrock knowledge bases automate it.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A Redshift fact table with billions of rows is joined constantly to a large customer dimension on customer id, and queries are slow because of data movement. What should the engineer change? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. key distribution on the join column co-locates matching rows on the same slices and avoids shuffling large tables. all on a huge table multiplies storage.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A DynamoDB table is keyed by shipment I D, and a new requirement is to list all shipments for a given customer sorted by date. What is the best solution? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A G S I provides a new key schema for the new query and can be added at any time. A scan is inefficient, and L S I s can only be created with the table.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Event producers occasionally add optional fields to Kafka messages, and existing consumers must keep working. Which approach enforces safe schema changes? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The Schema Registry versions schemas and rejects new versions that violate the chosen compatibility mode, protecting consumers.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A company migrates an Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. In what order should the work be done? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A heterogeneous migration converts the schema and code first, applies it to the target, and then moves data with D M S full load and change data capture.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A data lake in S three needs to add, rename and drop columns over time without rewriting existing files, and support time travel. Which approach fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Iceberg supports schema and partition evolution through table metadata and keeps snapshots for time travel.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Select two. Which two statements about a Bedrock knowledge base are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. The ingestion pipeline chunks and embeds documents, and retrieval embeds the question and adds similar chunks to the prompt. The model is not retrained.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. An auditor asks which source tables and jobs produced a figure in a report. Which capability answers this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Lineage records where data came from and how it was transformed; SageMaker Catalog provides lineage for assets, and M L Lineage Tracking covers M L workflows.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Select two. Athena queries on a large dataset scan far more data than needed. Which two changes reduce the data scanned? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Partitioning lets Athena skip folders and columnar Parquet lets it read only needed columns.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: A. Question two: C. Question three: C. Question four: C. Question five: C. Question six: B and D. Question seven: A. Question eight: B and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
